input.prompt:
/loop You are worker AI-CORE on Betterlook (task AI-CORE: the AI layer). Your progress file is `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3400.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-CORE), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

The Betterlook frontend shell is done (Astryx app: landing composer, then chat on the left and preview on the right). Now build the AI layer from scratch. My priority is not features. It's a clean AI integration that we can control and measure with evals. Work through it step by step until it's done.

The shape I want:

1. One agent core. A single runAgent() function on the server owns the whole loop: model call, tools, step limit, streaming. /api/chat uses it for the UI, and a CLI uses it for evals. Same code path, never a second implementation. Use the Vercel AI SDK (streamText with tools, stopWhen with a step limit, useChat on the client). No agent framework on top.

2. One shared types file (lib/agent/types.ts) that the UI, the runner and later the database all import: the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call and the event types (restore, keep, approve, deny). Write it early and keep it the single source of truth. [Also `ProviderCredential` per the shared contract, shaped so an OAuth access token from AUTH fits beside an API key. Commit a first version of the real file at the end of your Plan item, not only a draft in the progress file: AI-UI and AUTH build against it. After that, any change to it is announced in your progress file under "types.ts changes".]

3. Explicit controls, all in one config file I can read at a glance:
   - tool allowlist (start with: list files, read file, search, edit file via search/replace, write file, typecheck; no shell, no web, no installs)
   - max steps and max output tokens per turn
   - a path policy: tools can only touch the project folder in the sandbox, and edits to package.json, lockfiles or config files need the user's approval
   - every tool call goes through one policy check before it runs; denied calls go back to the model as a tool error and get logged; protected-file edits pause the turn and wait for approve/deny from the UI
   - prompt caching on, so we don't waste the user's tokens

4. Checkpoint and verify after every turn:
   - the sandbox project is a git repo; commit after each agent turn so any turn can be restored
   - when a turn ends, run a verify step: typecheck, build, and runtime errors from the preview (console and page errors)
   - if verify fails, give the agent exactly one repair attempt with the errors; if it still fails, mark the turn as failed and offer restore. Never loop forever.
   - restore, keep, approve and deny are logged as events (I'll use them as preference signals later)

5. Traces built for evals. Every turn produces one turn record and sends it to Langfuse through the AI SDK telemetry: trace id, model and provider, system prompt hash, tool config hash, each tool call with arguments, result, allowed/denied and timing, token usage and cost, the git diff of the turn, files touched, verify results, repair attempt, final status and checkpoint id. Mask keys and env secrets before anything leaves the server. Editing the prompt or tool config must change its hash so scores never get mixed across versions.

6. Headless runner. `bun run agent:run --tasks <file> --runs <k>` starts a fresh sandbox per run, calls the same runAgent() with each task prompt, and writes one folder per run: the turn record, the diff, before/after screenshots of the preview, and verify results. It runs in parallel with a small concurrency cap, backs off on rate limits, and uses our own eval key from .env, never a user's key. It must not share a rate-limit budget with interactive use.

Things that are mine, not yours: the system prompt (leave a one-line placeholder in one file and tell me where), the task files, and anything that judges quality: rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, and any prompt-injection test cases. Build the plumbing so I can plug those in; don't write them.

Users bring their own key. Start with one provider through its official AI SDK provider package, and keep adding a second one a small change, but don't build the second yet. Never print, log, commit or put a key into a trace, error or screenshot. Don't type keys or create accounts yourself; ask me. [A separate worker, AUTH, is researching sign-in with existing subscriptions such as a ChatGPT account; your BYOK path must accept a `ProviderCredential` so AUTH's credential can plug in without changing runAgent().]

Keep it minimal: fewest dependencies, no abstractions we don't need yet, no UX changes beyond showing real messages, tool activity, verify status, approvals and restore. While there's no database, keep the current sandbox id and chat history in localStorage. [The rich UI for tool activity, verify, approvals and restore is AI-UI's; you expose the data and a minimal plain rendering until AI-UI wires in.]

Every time this loop runs:
- Open `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. If it doesn't exist, create it with this checklist and stop for this round:
  [ ] Plan: use the agent-reach skill to compare E2B, Vercel Sandbox and Daytona (isolation, preview URL, file API, git support, startup time, cost). Write the comparison, your pick, the runAgent() flow in 5-10 lines, and a draft of lib/agent/types.ts [committed as the real file]. Ask me: which sandbox, which first provider, and where the user's key lives (my default: in the browser, sent per request, used for that call only, never stored server-side). Stop and wait for me.
  [ ] Agent core, text only: lib/agent/types.ts committed; runAgent() streams replies into the chat panel; model picker, stop button and step limit work.
  [ ] BYOK: the key flows the way I picked; missing or wrong key shows a clear message.
  [ ] Turn record and tracing: each turn lands in Langfuse with the fields above; prompt and tool config hashes change when I edit them; no secret appears in an exported trace.
  [ ] Sandbox and preview: a fresh sandbox from a minimal React starter, initialized as a git repo; the preview shows it; reload reconnects to the same sandbox.
  [ ] Tools and policy: the allowlisted tools work; a call outside the project folder is denied, logged and returned to the model as a tool error; a package.json edit pauses for approval.
  [ ] Checkpoint and verify: commit per turn, verify after each turn, one repair attempt, failed-turn state, restore works, events logged.
  [ ] Headless runner: agent:run on a two-task sample file I'll give you produces complete run folders, 2 runs each, through the same runAgent().
  [ ] End to end: "make the hero heading blue" from the landing screen edits the code, verify passes, the preview turns blue, and the trace has every tool call, the diff and the checkpoint id.
  [ ] Failure states: rate limit, provider error, sandbox down, denied tool, failed verify and step limit each show a readable message, and the chat keeps working.
- Do only the first unchecked item.
- Prove it before ticking it: `bun run typecheck` passes; screenshots for UI steps that you've looked at yourself; the shortest log lines or trace excerpt for everything else; and a grep of logs, screenshots and traces for any value from .env showing no match. Put the evidence under the item.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry in the same round. If the same item fails three rounds in a row, stop and tell me what's blocking.
- If you need a key, an account, a decision, or you're tempted to write anything that judges quality, write the question in the progress file, stop and ask [by ending with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED].
- Pace the loop at 60 seconds between rounds.
- When everything is checked, stop and give me: screenshots of the end-to-end run and its trace id, one sample run folder from agent:run, the files and dependencies you added and why, what you skipped, and what felt fragile.

Standing orchestrator rules (founder answers, 2026-11-18): Sandbox = Vercel Sandbox. First provider = OpenAI via @ai-sdk/openai (Responses API, store:false); Anthropic is the later "small change". User key: browser, per request, never stored or logged server-side. Credential contract: browser sends API-key credentials in the request body as `credential` (from AUTH's `lib/auth/client.ts` `getCredential()`, stubbed until it lands); /api/chat resolves `parseCredential(body.credential) ?? await getServerCredential(req)` (AUTH's `lib/auth/server.ts`, stubbed until it lands). NO .env yet: build each item fully, prove with typecheck twice plus `bun test` unit tests using the `ai/test` mock language model and pure-logic tests; where a live proof needs credentials write "LIVE PROOF PENDING ENV: <exact check>" under the item, add it to "Pending e2e", and tick it. Item 2 (agent core, text only) is ticked and committed as `656d3991`. The two priority changes you asked for are separate commits, ready to merge.

**Ready to merge to `betterlook`:**
- **`0dccdb9a` feat(agent): add openai provider id.** `ProviderId` is now `'openai' | 'anthropic'` (I kept `anthropic` for the second provider), so AUTH is unblocked.
- **`4b0d0036` feat(agent): add allowed model list and validate requests against it.** `lib/agent/models.ts` is plain data with `{id, label, provider}` per model and no server-only imports, so the client can import it.
  - I listed `gpt-5.5` first as the default, then `gpt-5`. Both ids are known to `@ai-sdk/openai`, but I picked them myself, so the founder may want a different set.
  - `/api/chat` rejects any model not in the list.
  - I never edited anything under `composer/`. Until AI-UI's picker imports the new list, the workspace still defaults to Claude from `composer/models.ts`, and picking a non-OpenAI model shows "<model> is not connected yet."

**What item 2 delivers:**
- `runAgent()` streams replies into the chat panel, with a step limit of 20 and an 8,000-token output cap.
- The model picker decides which model each request uses, and the Stop button cancels the request.
- The credential travels in the request body. `/api/chat` uses the body's credential, then falls back to `getServerCredential(req)`. Both AUTH functions are one-line stubs returning null until AUTH's files land.
- The system prompt slot for the founder is `lib/agent/system-prompt.ts`. It is empty, and empty sends no instructions.
- A missing credential shows "Sign in or add an API key to start.", and the chat keeps working after that error.

**How it was checked:** typecheck and `bun test` (5 mock-model tests) passed in two separate runs, and React Doctor scored 100/100.
- **Step limit:** a mock model that keeps calling tools stops at exactly 20 steps.
- **Stop and streaming:** shown in screenshots with `/api/chat` mocked in the browser.
- **Real route:** screenshots show the "not connected yet" and missing-credential messages, and that the picker changes the model sent.

**Not yet proven:**
- A real streamed OpenAI reply, and Stop aborting the request on the server, need a key. I logged it as LIVE PROOF PENDING ENV under the item and in "Pending e2e".
- Reloading the workspace sends the landing prompt again. Chat history moves to localStorage in the Sandbox item.

**Added:**
- `@ai-sdk/openai@4.0.121`, the first provider.
- `@ai-sdk/react@4.0.180` for `useChat`.
- `@types/bun@1.4.4` as a dev dependency so typecheck understands the test file.
- A `test` script in both `package.json` files.

One thing that took debugging: `useChat`'s built-in chat stops itself during React's dev-mode double mount, which silently dropped the first message. `Workspace.tsx` now owns the chat instance instead.

The next round starts BYOK in about 90 seconds; the loop keeps going on its own.

/loop You are worker AI-CORE on Betterlook (task AI-CORE: the AI layer). Your progress file is `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3400.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-CORE), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

The Betterlook frontend shell is done (Astryx app: landing composer, then chat on the left and preview on the right). Now build the AI layer from scratch. My priority is not features. It's a clean AI integration that we can control and measure with evals. Work through it step by step until it's done.

The shape I want:

1. One agent core. A single runAgent() function on the server owns the whole loop: model call, tools, step limit, streaming. /api/chat uses it for the UI, and a CLI uses it for evals. Same code path, never a second implementation. Use the Vercel AI SDK (streamText with tools, stopWhen with a step limit, useChat on the client). No agent framework on top.

2. One shared types file (lib/agent/types.ts) that the UI, the runner and later the database all import: the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call and the event types (restore, keep, approve, deny). Write it early and keep it the single source of truth. [Also `ProviderCredential` per the shared contract, shaped so an OAuth access token from AUTH fits beside an API key. Commit a first version of the real file at the end of your Plan item, not only a draft in the progress file: AI-UI and AUTH build against it. After that, any change to it is announced in your progress file under "types.ts changes".]

3. Explicit controls, all in one config file I can read at a glance:
   - tool allowlist (start with: list files, read file, search, edit file via search/replace, write file, typecheck; no shell, no web, no installs)
   - max steps and max output tokens per turn
   - a path policy: tools can only touch the project folder in the sandbox, and edits to package.json, lockfiles or config files need the user's approval
   - every tool call goes through one policy check before it runs; denied calls go back to the model as a tool error and get logged; protected-file edits pause the turn and wait for approve/deny from the UI
   - prompt caching on, so we don't waste the user's tokens

4. Checkpoint and verify after every turn:
   - the sandbox project is a git repo; commit after each agent turn so any turn can be restored
   - when a turn ends, run a verify step: typecheck, build, and runtime errors from the preview (console and page errors)
   - if verify fails, give the agent exactly one repair attempt with the errors; if it still fails, mark the turn as failed and offer restore. Never loop forever.
   - restore, keep, approve and deny are logged as events (I'll use them as preference signals later)

5. Traces built for evals. Every turn produces one turn record and sends it to Langfuse through the AI SDK telemetry: trace id, model and provider, system prompt hash, tool config hash, each tool call with arguments, result, allowed/denied and timing, token usage and cost, the git diff of the turn, files touched, verify results, repair attempt, final status and checkpoint id. Mask keys and env secrets before anything leaves the server. Editing the prompt or tool config must change its hash so scores never get mixed across versions.

6. Headless runner. `bun run agent:run --tasks <file> --runs <k>` starts a fresh sandbox per run, calls the same runAgent() with each task prompt, and writes one folder per run: the turn record, the diff, before/after screenshots of the preview, and verify results. It runs in parallel with a small concurrency cap, backs off on rate limits, and uses our own eval key from .env, never a user's key. It must not share a rate-limit budget with interactive use.

Things that are mine, not yours: the system prompt (leave a one-line placeholder in one file and tell me where), the task files, and anything that judges quality: rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, and any prompt-injection test cases. Build the plumbing so I can plug those in; don't write them.

Users bring their own key. Start with one provider through its official AI SDK provider package, and keep adding a second one a small change, but don't build the second yet. Never print, log, commit or put a key into a trace, error or screenshot. Don't type keys or create accounts yourself; ask me. [A separate worker, AUTH, is researching sign-in with existing subscriptions such as a ChatGPT account; your BYOK path must accept a `ProviderCredential` so AUTH's credential can plug in without changing runAgent().]

Keep it minimal: fewest dependencies, no abstractions we don't need yet, no UX changes beyond showing real messages, tool activity, verify status, approvals and restore. While there's no database, keep the current sandbox id and chat history in localStorage. [The rich UI for tool activity, verify, approvals and restore is AI-UI's; you expose the data and a minimal plain rendering until AI-UI wires in.]

Every time this loop runs:
- Open `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. If it doesn't exist, create it with this checklist and stop for this round:
  [ ] Plan: use the agent-reach skill to compare E2B, Vercel Sandbox and Daytona (isolation, preview URL, file API, git support, startup time, cost). Write the comparison, your pick, the runAgent() flow in 5-10 lines, and a draft of lib/agent/types.ts [committed as the real file]. Ask me: which sandbox, which first provider, and where the user's key lives (my default: in the browser, sent per request, used for that call only, never stored server-side). Stop and wait for me.
  [ ] Agent core, text only: lib/agent/types.ts committed; runAgent() streams replies into the chat panel; model picker, stop button and step limit work.
  [ ] BYOK: the key flows the way I picked; missing or wrong key shows a clear message.
  [ ] Turn record and tracing: each turn lands in Langfuse with the fields above; prompt and tool config hashes change when I edit them; no secret appears in an exported trace.
  [ ] Sandbox and preview: a fresh sandbox from a minimal React starter, initialized as a git repo; the preview shows it; reload reconnects to the same sandbox.
  [ ] Tools and policy: the allowlisted tools work; a call outside the project folder is denied, logged and returned to the model as a tool error; a package.json edit pauses for approval.
  [ ] Checkpoint and verify: commit per turn, verify after each turn, one repair attempt, failed-turn state, restore works, events logged.
  [ ] Headless runner: agent:run on a two-task sample file I'll give you produces complete run folders, 2 runs each, through the same runAgent().
  [ ] End to end: "make the hero heading blue" from the landing screen edits the code, verify passes, the preview turns blue, and the trace has every tool call, the diff and the checkpoint id.
  [ ] Failure states: rate limit, provider error, sandbox down, denied tool, failed verify and step limit each show a readable message, and the chat keeps working.
- Do only the first unchecked item.
- Prove it before ticking it: `bun run typecheck` passes; screenshots for UI steps that you've looked at yourself; the shortest log lines or trace excerpt for everything else; and a grep of logs, screenshots and traces for any value from .env showing no match. Put the evidence under the item.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry in the same round. If the same item fails three rounds in a row, stop and tell me what's blocking.
- If you need a key, an account, a decision, or you're tempted to write anything that judges quality, write the question in the progress file, stop and ask [by ending with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED].
- Pace the loop at 60 seconds between rounds.
- When everything is checked, stop and give me: screenshots of the end-to-end run and its trace id, one sample run folder from agent:run, the files and dependencies you added and why, what you skipped, and what felt fragile.

Standing orchestrator rules (founder answers, 2026-11-18): Sandbox = Vercel Sandbox. First provider = OpenAI via @ai-sdk/openai (Responses API, store:false); Anthropic is the later "small change". User key: browser, per request, never stored or logged server-side. Credential contract: browser sends API-key credentials in the request body as `credential` (from AUTH's `lib/auth/client.ts` `getCredential()`, stubbed until it lands); /api/chat resolves `parseCredential(body.credential) ?? await getServerCredential(req)` (AUTH's `lib/auth/server.ts`, stubbed until it lands). NO .env yet: build each item fully, prove with typecheck twice plus `bun test` unit tests using the `ai/test` mock language model and pure-logic tests; where a live proof needs credentials write "LIVE PROOF PENDING ENV: <exact check>" under the item, add it to "Pending e2e", and tick it. Stop before the Headless runner item if no task file has been given, and stop before End to end. Do not create accounts.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.

Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.

input.prompt:
/loop You are worker AI-CORE on Betterlook (task AI-CORE: the AI layer). Your progress file is `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3400.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-CORE), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

The Betterlook frontend shell is done (Astryx app: landing composer, then chat on the left and preview on the right). Now build the AI layer from scratch. My priority is not features. It's a clean AI integration that we can control and measure with evals. Work through it step by step until it's done.

The shape I want:

1. One agent core. A single runAgent() function on the server owns the whole loop: model call, tools, step limit, streaming. /api/chat uses it for the UI, and a CLI uses it for evals. Same code path, never a second implementation. Use the Vercel AI SDK (streamText with tools, stopWhen with a step limit, useChat on the client). No agent framework on top.

2. One shared types file (lib/agent/types.ts) that the UI, the runner and later the database all import: the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call and the event types (restore, keep, approve, deny). Write it early and keep it the single source of truth. [Also `ProviderCredential` per the shared contract, shaped so an OAuth access token from AUTH fits beside an API key. Commit a first version of the real file at the end of your Plan item, not only a draft in the progress file: AI-UI and AUTH build against it. After that, any change to it is announced in your progress file under "types.ts changes".]

3. Explicit controls, all in one config file I can read at a glance:
   - tool allowlist (start with: list files, read file, search, edit file via search/replace, write file, typecheck; no shell, no web, no installs)
   - max steps and max output tokens per turn
   - a path policy: tools can only touch the project folder in the sandbox, and edits to package.json, lockfiles or config files need the user's approval
   - every tool call goes through one policy check before it runs; denied calls go back to the model as a tool error and get logged; protected-file edits pause the turn and wait for approve/deny from the UI
   - prompt caching on, so we don't waste the user's tokens

4. Checkpoint and verify after every turn:
   - the sandbox project is a git repo; commit after each agent turn so any turn can be restored
   - when a turn ends, run a verify step: typecheck, build, and runtime errors from the preview (console and page errors)
   - if verify fails, give the agent exactly one repair attempt with the errors; if it still fails, mark the turn as failed and offer restore. Never loop forever.
   - restore, keep, approve and deny are logged as events (I'll use them as preference signals later)

5. Traces built for evals. Every turn produces one turn record and sends it to Langfuse through the AI SDK telemetry: trace id, model and provider, system prompt hash, tool config hash, each tool call with arguments, result, allowed/denied and timing, token usage and cost, the git diff of the turn, files touched, verify results, repair attempt, final status and checkpoint id. Mask keys and env secrets before anything leaves the server. Editing the prompt or tool config must change its hash so scores never get mixed across versions.

6. Headless runner. `bun run agent:run --tasks <file> --runs <k>` starts a fresh sandbox per run, calls the same runAgent() with each task prompt, and writes one folder per run: the turn record, the diff, before/after screenshots of the preview, and verify results. It runs in parallel with a small concurrency cap, backs off on rate limits, and uses our own eval key from .env, never a user's key. It must not share a rate-limit budget with interactive use.

Things that are mine, not yours: the system prompt (leave a one-line placeholder in one file and tell me where), the task files, and anything that judges quality: rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, and any prompt-injection test cases. Build the plumbing so I can plug those in; don't write them.

Users bring their own key. Start with one provider through its official AI SDK provider package, and keep adding a second one a small change, but don't build the second yet. Never print, log, commit or put a key into a trace, error or screenshot. Don't type keys or create accounts yourself; ask me. [A separate worker, AUTH, is researching sign-in with existing subscriptions such as a ChatGPT account; your BYOK path must accept a `ProviderCredential` so AUTH's credential can plug in without changing runAgent().]

Keep it minimal: fewest dependencies, no abstractions we don't need yet, no UX changes beyond showing real messages, tool activity, verify status, approvals and restore. While there's no database, keep the current sandbox id and chat history in localStorage. [The rich UI for tool activity, verify, approvals and restore is AI-UI's; you expose the data and a minimal plain rendering until AI-UI wires in.]

Every time this loop runs:
- Open `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. If it doesn't exist, create it with this checklist and stop for this round:
  [ ] Plan: use the agent-reach skill to compare E2B, Vercel Sandbox and Daytona (isolation, preview URL, file API, git support, startup time, cost). Write the comparison, your pick, the runAgent() flow in 5-10 lines, and a draft of lib/agent/types.ts [committed as the real file]. Ask me: which sandbox, which first provider, and where the user's key lives (my default: in the browser, sent per request, used for that call only, never stored server-side). Stop and wait for me.
  [ ] Agent core, text only: lib/agent/types.ts committed; runAgent() streams replies into the chat panel; model picker, stop button and step limit work.
  [ ] BYOK: the key flows the way I picked; missing or wrong key shows a clear message.
  [ ] Turn record and tracing: each turn lands in Langfuse with the fields above; prompt and tool config hashes change when I edit them; no secret appears in an exported trace.
  [ ] Sandbox and preview: a fresh sandbox from a minimal React starter, initialized as a git repo; the preview shows it; reload reconnects to the same sandbox.
  [ ] Tools and policy: the allowlisted tools work; a call outside the project folder is denied, logged and returned to the model as a tool error; a package.json edit pauses for approval.
  [ ] Checkpoint and verify: commit per turn, verify after each turn, one repair attempt, failed-turn state, restore works, events logged.
  [ ] Headless runner: agent:run on a two-task sample file I'll give you produces complete run folders, 2 runs each, through the same runAgent().
  [ ] End to end: "make the hero heading blue" from the landing screen edits the code, verify passes, the preview turns blue, and the trace has every tool call, the diff and the checkpoint id.
  [ ] Failure states: rate limit, provider error, sandbox down, denied tool, failed verify and step limit each show a readable message, and the chat keeps working.
- Do only the first unchecked item.
- Prove it before ticking it: `bun run typecheck` passes; screenshots for UI steps that you've looked at yourself; the shortest log lines or trace excerpt for everything else; and a grep of logs, screenshots and traces for any value from .env showing no match. Put the evidence under the item.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry in the same round. If the same item fails three rounds in a row, stop and tell me what's blocking.
- If you need a key, an account, a decision, or you're tempted to write anything that judges quality, write the question in the progress file, stop and ask [by ending with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED].
- Pace the loop at 60 seconds between rounds.
- When everything is checked, stop and give me: screenshots of the end-to-end run and its trace id, one sample run folder from agent:run, the files and dependencies you added and why, what you skipped, and what felt fragile.

Standing orchestrator rules (founder answers, 2026-11-18): Sandbox = Vercel Sandbox. First provider = OpenAI via @ai-sdk/openai (Responses API, store:false); Anthropic is the later "small change". User key: browser, per request, never stored or logged server-side. Credential contract: browser sends API-key credentials in the request body as `credential` (from AUTH's `lib/auth/client.ts` `getCredential()`, stubbed until it lands); /api/chat resolves `parseCredential(body.credential) ?? await getServerCredential(req)` (AUTH's `lib/auth/server.ts`, stubbed until it lands). Allowed models live in `lib/agent/models.ts` (plain data, client-safe); never edit `composer/`. NO .env yet: build each item fully, prove with typecheck twice plus `bun test` unit tests using the `ai/test` mock language model and pure-logic tests; where a live proof needs credentials write "LIVE PROOF PENDING ENV: <exact check>" under the item, add it to "Pending e2e", and tick it. Stop before the Headless runner item if no task file has been given, and stop before End to end. Do not create accounts.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.

   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). input.prompt:
/loop You are worker AI-CORE on Betterlook (task AI-CORE: the AI layer). Your progress file is `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3400.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-CORE), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

The Betterlook frontend shell is done (Astryx app: landing composer, then chat on the left and preview on the right). Now build the AI layer from scratch. My priority is not features. It's a clean AI integration that we can control and measure with evals. Work through it step by step until it's done.

The shape I want:

1. One agent core. A single runAgent() function on the server owns the whole loop: model call, tools, step limit, streaming. /api/chat uses it for the UI, and a CLI uses it for evals. Same code path, never a second implementation. Use the Vercel AI SDK (streamText with tools, stopWhen with a step limit, useChat on the client). No agent framework on top.

2. One shared types file (lib/agent/types.ts) that the UI, the runner and later the database all import: the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call and the event types (restore, keep, approve, deny). Write it early and keep it the single source of truth. [Also `ProviderCredential` per the shared contract, shaped so an OAuth access token from AUTH fits beside an API key. Commit a first version of the real file at the end of your Plan item, not only a draft in the progress file: AI-UI and AUTH build against it. After that, any change to it is announced in your progress file under "types.ts changes".]

3. Explicit controls, all in one config file I can read at a glance:
   - tool allowlist (start with: list files, read file, search, edit file via search/replace, write file, typecheck; no shell, no web, no installs)
   - max steps and max output tokens per turn
   - a path policy: tools can only touch the project folder in the sandbox, and edits to package.json, lockfiles or config files need the user's approval
   - every tool call goes through one policy check before it runs; denied calls go back to the model as a tool error and get logged; protected-file edits pause the turn and wait for approve/deny from the UI
   - prompt caching on, so we don't waste the user's tokens

4. Checkpoint and verify after every turn:
   - the sandbox project is a git repo; commit after each agent turn so any turn can be restored
   - when a turn ends, run a verify step: typecheck, build, and runtime errors from the preview (console and page errors)
   - if verify fails, give the agent exactly one repair attempt with the errors; if it still fails, mark the turn as failed and offer restore. Never loop forever.
   - restore, keep, approve and deny are logged as events (I'll use them as preference signals later)

5. Traces built for evals. Every turn produces one turn record and sends it to Langfuse through the AI SDK telemetry: trace id, model and provider, system prompt hash, tool config hash, each tool call with arguments, result, allowed/denied and timing, token usage and cost, the git diff of the turn, files touched, verify results, repair attempt, final status and checkpoint id. Mask keys and env secrets before anything leaves the server. Editing the prompt or tool config must change its hash so scores never get mixed across versions.

6. Headless runner. `bun run agent:run --tasks <file> --runs <k>` starts a fresh sandbox per run, calls the same runAgent() with each task prompt, and writes one folder per run: the turn record, the diff, before/after screenshots of the preview, and verify results. It runs in parallel with a small concurrency cap, backs off on rate limits, and uses our own eval key from .env, never a user's key. It must not share a rate-limit budget with interactive use.

Things that are mine, not yours: the system prompt (leave a one-line placeholder in one file and tell me where), the task files, and anything that judges quality: rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, and any prompt-injection test cases. Build the plumbing so I can plug those in; don't write them.

Users bring their own key. Start with one provider through its official AI SDK provider package, and keep adding a second one a small change, but don't build the second yet. Never print, log, commit or put a key into a trace, error or screenshot. Don't type keys or create accounts yourself; ask me. [A separate worker, AUTH, is researching sign-in with existing subscriptions such as a ChatGPT account; your BYOK path must accept a `ProviderCredential` so AUTH's credential can plug in without changing runAgent().]

Keep it minimal: fewest dependencies, no abstractions we don't need yet, no UX changes beyond showing real messages, tool activity, verify status, approvals and restore. While there's no database, keep the current sandbox id and chat history in localStorage. [The rich UI for tool activity, verify, approvals and restore is AI-UI's; you expose the data and a minimal plain rendering until AI-UI wires in.]

Every time this loop runs:
- Open `ai-progress.md` at the repo root. If it doesn't exist, create it with this checklist and stop for this round:
  [ ] Plan: use the agent-reach skill to compare E2B, Vercel Sandbox and Daytona (isolation, preview URL, file API, git support, startup time, cost). Write the comparison, your pick, the runAgent() flow in 5-10 lines, and a draft of lib/agent/types.ts [committed as the real file]. Ask me: which sandbox, which first provider, and where the user's key lives (my default: in the browser, sent per request, used for that call only, never stored server-side). Stop and wait for me.
  [ ] Agent core, text only: lib/agent/types.ts committed; runAgent() streams replies into the chat panel; model picker, stop button and step limit work.
  [ ] BYOK: the key flows the way I picked; missing or wrong key shows a clear message.
